guidance.title: Cellulitis and Cutaneous Abscess
guidance.summary:
### Discharge Criteria
- Mild cellulitis: immunocompetent, no systemic signs, reliable follow-up
- Abscess after I&D: pain controlled, no surrounding cellulitis/systemic signs, able to return for wound check in 48-72 hours
- Prescribe oral antibiotics, wound care instructions, clear return precautions

### Admission Criteria
- Systemic toxicity (fever, tachycardia, hypotension)
- Failed outpatient oral antibiotics (progression despite 48-72 hours of therapy)
- Immunocompromised (diabetes, HIV, transplant, chemotherapy)
- Extensive cellulitis requiring IV antibiotics
- Location requiring close monitoring (face, orbit, hand, perineum)
- Concern for necrotizing fasciitis or deep space infection — surgical consultation and admission
- Unable to tolerate oral medications

### Follow-Up
- Wound check 48-72 hours post-I&D
- Cellulitis re-evaluation at 48-72 hours to assess response (erythema should not extend beyond marked borders)
- Return immediately for: increasing pain, expanding erythema beyond marks, fever, systemic symptoms, crepitus, skin color change to dusky/purple

guidance.title: Cellulitis and Cutaneous Abscess
guidance.summary:
### Cellulitis (Non-Purulent SSTI)
- Spreading erythema, warmth, edema, tenderness without drainable collection
- Poorly defined borders, often unilateral
- Entry point: skin break, wound, tinea pedis, insect bite
- Most common pathogen: Group A Streptococcus (GAS), also Staphylococcus aureus
- Systemic signs: fever, tachycardia, lymphangitis, regional lymphadenopathy

### Cutaneous Abscess (Purulent SSTI)
- Fluctuant, tender, erythematous mass with overlying warmth
- Point tenderness, may have spontaneous drainage
- Most common pathogen: MRSA (prevalence 50-75% in community abscesses in the US)
- Common locations: axilla, groin, perirectal, buttock, face

### Severity Classification (IDSA)
| Class | Description | Management |
|---|---|---|
| Mild | No systemic signs, immunocompetent | Outpatient oral antibiotics or I&D alone |
| Moderate | Systemic signs (fever, tachycardia, WBC >12 or <4) OR immunocompromised OR failed outpatient therapy | IV antibiotics, observation or admit |
| Severe | Failed IV antibiotics, sepsis, deep space infection, necrotizing fasciitis | Surgical consultation, ICU |

### LRINEC Score (Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis)
| Parameter | Criteria | Points |
|---|---|---|
| CRP | ≥ 150 mg/L | 4 |
| WBC | 15-25 × 10⁹/L | 1 |
| WBC | > 25 × 10⁹/L | 2 |
| Hemoglobin | 11-13.5 g/dL | 1 |
| Hemoglobin | < 11 g/dL | 2 |
| Sodium | < 135 mEq/L | 2 |
| Creatinine | > 1.6 mg/dL | 2 |
| Glucose | > 180 mg/dL | 1 |

- Score ≥ 6: Intermediate/high risk for necrotizing fasciitis — surgical consultation
- Score ≥ 8: Strongly predictive — proceed to OR
- Sensitivity is imperfect (68-92%); clinical suspicion overrides a low score

guidance.title: Orbital Cellulitis
guidance.summary:
1. **Misdiagnosing orbital cellulitis as preseptal cellulitis.** Any proptosis, EOM restriction, or vision change mandates CT and IV antibiotics. Oral antibiotics alone for true orbital cellulitis leads to vision loss and intracranial complications.

2. **Failing to obtain CT with contrast.** Non-contrast CT misses early abscess formation and subperiosteal collections. Contrast is essential.

3. **Not performing serial visual acuity checks.** Vision can deteriorate rapidly from optic nerve compression. Declining acuity or a new afferent pupillary defect is a surgical emergency — do not wait for repeat imaging.

4. **Missing intracranial complications.** Cavernous sinus thrombosis presents with bilateral orbital findings, cranial nerve palsies, and meningismus. Requires MRI/MRV and neurosurgical involvement.

5. **Inadequate anaerobic coverage.** Sinus-source orbital cellulitis often involves polymicrobial flora including anaerobes. Omitting metronidazole increases treatment failure risk.

6. **Missing mucormycosis in immunocompromised patients.** Diabetics in DKA or neutropenic patients with orbital cellulitis must be evaluated for invasive fungal sinusitis — requires urgent biopsy and amphotericin B.

guidance.title: Peptic Ulcer
guidance.summary:
A peptic ulcer is a sore in the lining of your stomach or your duodenum, the first part of your small intestine. A burning stomach pain is the most common symptom. The pain: 
 Starts between meals or during the night 
 Briefly stops if you eat or take antacids 
 Lasts for minutes to hours 
 Comes and goes for several days or weeks 
 

 Peptic ulcers happen when the acids that help you digest food damage the walls of the stomach or duodenum. The most common cause is infection with a bacterium called Helicobacter pylori . Another cause is the long-term use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medicines (NSAIDs) such as aspirin and ibuprofen. Stress and spicy foods do not cause ulcers, but can make them worse. 

 To see if you have an H. pylori infection, your doctor will test your blood, breath, or stool. Your doctor also may look inside your stomach and duodenum by doing an endoscopy or x-ray. 

 Peptic ulcers will get worse if not treated. Treatment may include medicines to reduce stomach acids or antibiotics to kill H. pylori. Antacids and milk can't heal peptic ulcers. Not smoking and avoiding alcohol can help. You may need surgery if your ulcers don't heal.

A peptic ulcer is a sore in the lining of your stomach or your duodenum, the first part of your small intestine. A burning stomach pain is the most common symptom. The pain: 
 Starts between meals or during the night 
 Briefly stops if you eat or take antacids 
 Lasts for minutes to hours 
 Comes and goes for several days or weeks 
 

 Peptic ulcers happen when the acids that help you digest food damage the walls of the stomach or duodenum. The most common cause is infection with a bacterium called Helicobacter pylori . Another cause is the long-term use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medicines (NSAIDs) such as aspirin and ibuprofen. Stress and spicy foods do not cause ulcers, but can make them worse. 

 To see if you have an H. pylori infection, your doctor will test your blood, breath, or stool. Your doctor also may look inside your stomach and duodenum by doing an endoscopy or x-ray. 

 Peptic ulcers will get worse if not treated. Treatment may include medicines to reduce stomach acids or antibiotics to kill H. pylori. Antacids and milk can't heal peptic ulcers. Not smoking and avoiding alcohol can help. You may need surgery if your ulcers don't heal.

guidance.summary:
**Presentation:**
- Unilateral periorbital swelling, erythema, warmth
- Proptosis (distinguishes orbital from preseptal cellulitis)
- Pain with extraocular movements (pathognomonic)
- Ophthalmoplegia, restricted gaze
- Decreased visual acuity, afferent pupillary defect (optic nerve compromise)
- Fever, malaise, elevated WBC

- Decreased vision
- Chemosis

- Dental infection, dacryocystitis, skin infection
- Post-surgical, post-traumatic

guidance.title: Necrotizing Fasciitis — Skin Presentation
guidance.summary:
**Hard signs (any one is sufficient for operative exploration):**
- Crepitus on palpation (subcutaneous gas)
- Skin necrosis or dusky discoloration beyond erythema
- Bullae (hemorrhagic or serous)
- Gas on imaging (CT or X-ray)
- Dishwater-gray wound drainage
- Skin anesthesia within area of erythema (nerve destruction)
- Rapid progression of erythema despite IV antibiotics

**Soft signs (high suspicion when multiple present):**
- Pain out of proportion to skin findings (hallmark — most sensitive early sign)
- Wooden-hard induration of subcutaneous tissue
- Edema beyond area of erythema
- Systemic toxicity: high fever, tachycardia, hypotension
- Failure to improve with 24-48h of appropriate cellulitis antibiotics

**Classification:**
- **Type I (polymicrobial):** Mixed aerobic/anaerobic flora; occurs in diabetics, post-surgical, perineal (Fournier gangrene)
- **Type II (monomicrobial):** Group A Streptococcus (most common), Staphylococcus aureus, Vibrio vulnificus; occurs in otherwise healthy patients
- **Type III:** Clostridial gas gangrene (Clostridium perfringens); rapid gas formation, bronze skin

**LRINEC Score (Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis):**
- CRP >= 150 mg/L (+4)
- WBC 15-25k (+1), > 25k (+2)
- Hemoglobin < 13.5 (+1), < 11 (+2)
- Sodium < 135 (+2)
- Creatinine > 1.6 (+2)
- Glucose > 180 (+1)
- Score >= 6: High suspicion; Score >= 8: Strongly predictive
- NOTE: Low LRINEC does NOT rule out necrotizing fasciitis — clinical judgment supersedes scoring

1. **Misdiagnosing orbital cellulitis as preseptal cellulitis.** Any proptosis, EOM restriction, or vision change mandates CT and IV antibiotics. Oral antibiotics alone for true orbital cellulitis leads to vision loss and intracranial complications.

2. **Failing to obtain CT with contrast.** Non-contrast CT misses early abscess formation and subperiosteal collections. Contrast is essential.

3. **Not performing serial visual acuity checks.** Vision can deteriorate rapidly from optic nerve compression. Declining acuity or a new afferent pupillary defect is a surgical emergency — do not wait for repeat imaging.

4. **Missing intracranial complications.** Cavernous sinus thrombosis presents with bilateral orbital findings, cranial nerve palsies, and meningismus. Requires MRI/MRV and neurosurgical involvement.

5. **Inadequate anaerobic coverage.** Sinus-source orbital cellulitis often involves polymicrobial flora including anaerobes. Omitting metronidazole increases treatment failure risk.

6. **Missing mucormycosis in immunocompromised patients.** Diabetics in DKA or neutropenic patients with orbital cellulitis must be evaluated for invasive fungal sinusitis — requires urgent biopsy and amphotericin B.

A peptic ulcer is a sore in the lining of your stomach or your duodenum, the first part of your small intestine. A burning stomach pain is the most common symptom. The pain: 
 Starts between meals or during the night 
 Briefly stops if you eat or take antacids 
 Lasts for minutes to hours 
 Comes and goes for several days or weeks 
 

 Peptic ulcers happen when the acids that help you digest food damage the walls of the stomach or duodenum. The most common cause is infection with a bacterium called Helicobacter pylori . Another cause is the long-term use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medicines (NSAIDs) such as aspirin and ibuprofen. Stress and spicy foods do not cause ulcers, but can make them worse. 

 To see if you have an H. pylori infection, your doctor will test your blood, breath, or stool. Your doctor also may look inside your stomach and duodenum by doing an endoscopy or x-ray. 

 Peptic ulcers will get worse if not treated. Treatment may include medicines to reduce stomach acids or antibiotics to kill H. pylori. Antacids and milk can't heal peptic ulcers. Not smoking and avoiding alcohol can help. You may need surgery if your ulcers don't heal. 

 NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases

**Hard signs (any one is sufficient for operative exploration):**
- Crepitus on palpation (subcutaneous gas)
- Skin necrosis or dusky discoloration beyond erythema
- Bullae (hemorrhagic or serous)
- Gas on imaging (CT or X-ray)
- Dishwater-gray wound drainage
- Skin anesthesia within area of erythema (nerve destruction)
- Rapid progression of erythema despite IV antibiotics

**Soft signs (high suspicion when multiple present):**
- Pain out of proportion to skin findings (hallmark — most sensitive early sign)
- Wooden-hard induration of subcutaneous tissue
- Edema beyond area of erythema
- Systemic toxicity: high fever, tachycardia, hypotension
- Failure to improve with 24-48h of appropriate cellulitis antibiotics

**Classification:**
- **Type I (polymicrobial):** Mixed aerobic/anaerobic flora; occurs in diabetics, post-surgical, perineal (Fournier gangrene)
- **Type II (monomicrobial):** Group A Streptococcus (most common), Staphylococcus aureus, Vibrio vulnificus; occurs in otherwise healthy patients
- **Type III:** Clostridial gas gangrene (Clostridium perfringens); rapid gas formation, bronze skin

**LRINEC Score (Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis):**
- CRP >= 150 mg/L (+4)
- WBC 15-25k (+1), > 25k (+2)
- Hemoglobin < 13.5 (+1), < 11 (+2)
- Sodium < 135 (+2)
- Creatinine > 1.6 (+2)
- Glucose > 180 (+1)
- Score >= 6: High suspicion; Score >= 8: Strongly predictive
- NOTE: Low LRINEC does NOT rule out necrotizing fasciitis — clinical judgment supersedes scoring

1. **Treating as simple cellulitis.** Pain out of proportion to skin findings, systemic toxicity, and failure to improve on antibiotics are red flags. If any hard sign is present, proceed directly to operative exploration.

2. **Relying on a low LRINEC score to rule out necrotizing fasciitis.** The LRINEC score has limited sensitivity (~60-80%). Clinical suspicion must override scoring. When in doubt, take the patient to the OR.

3. **Delaying surgery for imaging.** CT and MRI can support the diagnosis but are neither 100% sensitive nor specific. If clinical suspicion is high, operative exploration is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Every hour of surgical delay increases mortality.

4. **Performing a single debridement and declaring the patient treated.** Necrotizing fasciitis requires serial debridements. The infection often extends beyond the initial operative field. Return to OR in 24-48h is standard.

5. **Omitting clindamycin.** Clindamycin inhibits toxin production at the ribosomal level. In GAS and Staphylococcal infections, toxin-mediated tissue destruction continues even after bactericidal antibiotics kill the organism. Clindamycin addresses this mechanism.

6. **Missing Fournier gangrene.** Perineal necrotizing fasciitis (Fournier gangrene) in diabetics or immunocompromised patients may present with subtle perineal pain and scrotal swelling. Digital rectal exam and perineal inspection are essential in patients with perineal/genital complaints and sepsis.
